“nikle” is repeated with a shift of tense/mood: in the first line it suggests a breath that must come out with each desire; in the second it means sighs that have already come out, and finally “kam nikle” means too few have come out. English cannot fully keep the same verb form doing all this work.

“khvāhish” (desire/wish) and “armān” (sigh/longing/sorrow) are related but not identical: the first is the want, the second is the emotional exhalation it produces. I used “wishes” and “sighs” to keep the movement from desire to sigh.

The couplet rests on a paradox: “bahut nikle” (many have come out) and “kam nikle” (few have come out) are both true because the desires are countless, so even many sighs are insufficient. I rendered “kam nikle” as “too few” to make the insufficiency clear.
The Sufi double meaning is possible: the desires may be worldly or divine, and the sighs may be both human grief and spiritual longing; the breath can also suggest life itself being spent in longing.
